source_read: PDF PDFs/Cannabis/Broyd_2016_CognitionSR.pdf, accepted manuscript, all 27 PDF pages (AM pp. 2-11 text, pp. 12-23 references, Figure 1 legend p. 23, Table 1 pp. 24-25, Table 2 p. 26, Figure 1 p. 27); Tables 1 and 2 checked on rendered pages. Supplements 1 and 2 (study-level data) not read.

claims.overstatement: No overstatement of Broyd. If anything the Broyd sentences understate the review's own lean toward persistence: they report Table 1's 'mixed' persistence ratings and the authors' suggestion that verbal memory may recover, but not the abstract (AM p. 3) or Table 2 (AM p. 26), which give likely persistent effects on attention and psychomotor function and possible persistent effects on verbal learning and memory. Table 1 itself rates attention persistence as mixed, so the review is internally inconsistent here; the claim's 'contested' status covers it.
claims.note: Every Broyd number in the statement and magnitude was recovered: 2004-2015 (January 2004 to February 2015); eighteen abstinence studies (more than 24 h), most often 21-35 days, few longer; eleven cross-sectional (7 days to more than 1 year; 9 in adolescents or young adults) and seven prospective (21 days to 4-8 years; two confounded by drug treatment); Table 1 persistence +- for verbal learning and memory (9), working memory (7), attention (10), planning-type executive functions (9), verbal fluency (4), + for psychomotor (6), - for other memory (4), time estimation (1) and decision making (3). '23 to 53 days' maps to refs 91 (23 days, adults), 65 (28 days), 67 (35 days) and 85 (53 days; working memory and risk taking); 'older adults abstinent more than 28 days' is ref 57 (AM p. 10 says >28 days, AM p. 7 says >=28 days, aged about 35-50). The adolescent prospective study is ref 79 (Fried 2005) and the 12-month cohort ref 66 (Tait 2011). Table 1's abstinence column cites 17 distinct studies against 18 in the text. Broyd presents Meier 2012 as IQ decline persisting after cessation or reduction of use in the past year (AM p. 10) and says cessation did not restore IQ (AM p. 9); the claim correctly declines that reading. The 'critically low' AMSTAR 2 label is the editors' rating, not Broyd's; it is consistent with what the main text shows (no protocol, two databases, no formal appraisal of included studies; search details only in Supplement 1).

anchors.locator: Abstract
anchors.extracted: Systematic review of empirical studies published January 2004 to February 2015 on acute and chronic cannabinoid effects on cognition and on persistence or recovery after abstinence.

anchors.locator: Abstract (continued)
anchors.extracted: Authors' summary: impaired verbal memory, attention and some executive functions may persist after prolonged abstinence; psychomotor function has some evidence of persistence after cessation; persistence or recovery across all domains is under-researched.

anchors.locator: Results > Memory > Verbal learning and memory (paragraph continued) and Working memory
anchors.extracted: Improvement (ref 63) or recovery (refs 55, 57, 64-66) of verbal learning and memory with abstinence in some studies or indices but not others (64, 65, 67); working-memory impairment persisted a few weeks in one study (65) but appears mostly to resolve with longer abstinence (55, 57, 35, 67, 85).

anchors.locator: Results > Attention, 1st paragraph
anchors.extracted: Users abstinent 23 days remained impaired relative to controls despite improving sustained and divided attention (ref 91); other abstinence studies found no difference from controls on broader attention measures (57, 63, 64, 79, 95); authors suggest attentional impairment may be residual and dissipate gradually as cannabinoids are cleared.

anchors.locator: Results > Psychomotor function; Executive function, 1st paragraph
anchors.extracted: Psychomotor function impaired in users abstinent 23 to 35 days (refs 57, 65, 67, 91), with a trend after 12 months (finger tapping, ref 64); three abstinence studies in younger samples found no executive-function differences from controls (65, 85, 95).

anchors.locator: Results > Executive function, 1st paragraph (continued)
anchors.extracted: Persistent executive dysfunction in users abstinent 28 days or more aged about 35-50 (ref 57); in twins abstinent 12 months aged 38-51 (ref 64) Block Design was the only significant difference from their co-twins who had not used.

anchors.locator: Discussion > Persistence or recovery of function with abstinence, 1st paragraph
anchors.extracted: Recovery after prolonged abstinence called contentious; 18 new studies with abstinence over 24 h, most often 21-35 days, few longer; 11 cross-sectional (former users abstinent 7 days to over 1 year; 9 in adolescents or young adults) and 7 prospective (21 days to 4-8 years of abstinence), 2 of them confounded by concomitant drug treatment.

anchors.locator: Discussion > Persistence or recovery of function with abstinence, 2nd paragraph
anchors.extracted: Cross-sectional: some attention, verbal and working-memory and psychomotor-speed deficits in adolescents abstinent 28 days (65) and 35 days (67), not on other measures; working memory and risk taking still impaired after 53 days (85); poorer verbal fluency in young adults abstinent up to 4 weeks (119); adults abstinent over 28 days impaired on executive function and information processing but not attention or working memory (57); twins discordant for use, abstinent over 12 months: Block Design impaired, trends for verbal recall and finger tapping, yet the authors argued against long-term effects (64).

anchors.locator: Discussion > Persistence or recovery of function with abstinence, 3rd paragraph
anchors.extracted: Only 2 prospective studies controlled premorbid function: adolescent former users did not differ from controls on any measure (79); Meier 2012 (60) described as IQ decline by 38 persisting after cessation or reduction of use in the past year. Verbal learning improved by 2 weeks, visual search still impaired at 3 weeks (55); adults improved over 8-23 days but stayed impaired versus controls (91); former heavy users abstinent 12 months or more improved versus continuing heavy users on immediate verbal memory and did not differ from people who had not used on any measure (66; three waves 4 years apart).

anchors.locator: Discussion > Persistence or recovery of function with abstinence, 4th paragraph
anchors.extracted: Some but not all recent studies suggest verbal learning and memory impairment may recover with prolonged abstinence; evidence for persistent dysfunction continues to emerge (sentence ends on AM p. 11).

anchors.locator: Table 1, 'Persistence with abstinence' and 'Number of studies ABSTINENCE' columns, memory, attention and psychomotor rows
anchors.extracted: Verbal learning and memory +- (9 abstinence studies); working memory +- (7); other memory - (4); attention +- (10); attentional bias na (none); psychomotor + (6).

anchors.locator: Table 1 (continued), executive function and decision-making rows; legend and footnote a
anchors.extracted: Planning, reasoning, interference control and problem solving +- (9); inhibition na (none); verbal fluency +- (4); time estimation - (1); decision making - (3). +- = mixed evidence, + = weak evidence from few studies, - = little or no evidence of impairment; ratings are the authors' subjective consensus weighing number and quality of studies.

anchors.locator: Table 2, 'Recovery of function with abstinence'
anchors.extracted: Summary lists likely persistent effects on attention and psychomotor function, possible persistent effects on verbal learning and memory, and evidence insufficient and mixed.

claims.overstatement: None. The claim keeps association language where Broyd writes 'impaired' throughout; 'nothing pooled' is correct (qualitative synthesis of 105 studies).
claims.note: All Broyd numbers recovered from Table 1 (chronic column): verbal learning and memory +++ (20), attention +++ (14), working memory +- (16), planning-type executive functions +- (23), inhibition +- (9), decision making +- (17), psychomotor + (10). '+++' is defined as strong and largely consistent evidence of impairment, and the footnote says the ratings are the authors' subjective consensus. 'More than half ... did not report IQ or education' matches 'more than 50% of studies' (AM p. 9). The frequency sentence (AM p. 8) cites the senior author's own earlier review (ref 20). Broyd's chronic samples span adolescents to adults aged about 35-50 and include occasional users in one study (ref 55), so they are broader than the claim's 'adolescents and young adults'; the claim attributes the ratings to 'people who use cannabis regularly', which is fair.

anchors.locator: Method
anchors.extracted: PRISMA-guided review; 105 studies included; group differences and associations with use measures synthesised qualitatively, nothing pooled.

anchors.locator: Results > Memory > Verbal learning and memory
anchors.extracted: Impaired verbal learning and memory consistently observed in chronic users including adolescents and young adults (two studies not), even occasional users (ref 55); associations with frequency, quantity, duration and age of onset reported.

anchors.locator: Results > Attention, 1st paragraph
anchors.extracted: Many studies report attention and processing-speed impairment in adolescent and adult users with a wide range of exposure; impairment may be residual and dissipate as cannabinoids clear.

anchors.locator: Discussion, 1st paragraph
anchors.extracted: In studies of chronic users, associations with frequency of use more likely reflect residual effects of acute or subchronic intoxication, with dose residual or cumulative effects, and with duration more persistent alterations (citing ref 20); about 75% of studies mainly male, gender tested in about 12%.

anchors.locator: Discussion > Specificity to cannabis and potential confounds, 1st and 2nd paragraphs
anchors.extracted: More than 50% of studies did not report IQ or years of education and many did not control premorbid functioning; many studies fail to report or account for alcohol, tobacco and other drug use; impairing effects mostly held after controlling other substance use, but not in all studies.

anchors.locator: Table 1, 'Chronic' column and 'Number of studies CHRONIC', memory, attention and psychomotor rows
anchors.extracted: Verbal learning and memory +++ (20 chronic studies); working memory +- (16); other memory +- (8); attention +++ (14); attentional bias +++ (7); psychomotor + (10).

anchors.locator: Table 1 (continued), executive and decision-making rows; legend and footnote a
anchors.extracted: Planning-type executive functions +- (23); inhibition +- (9); verbal fluency +- (6); time estimation - (1); decision making +- (17); +++ = strong and largely consistent evidence of impairment; ratings are subjective consensus of the authors.

claims.overstatement: None in the claim. Broyd itself reads Meier 2012 causally ('resulted in', AM p. 10), says specificity was 'determined by ruling out' recent use and other substance use, and that cessation did not restore IQ, without the multivariable attenuation or the socioeconomic critique; the claim's 'insufficient' and 'disputed' are the more cautious reading.
claims.note: No number in the claim comes from Broyd. Broyd's '~6 points' for persistent use or dependence matches the claim's 99.68 to 93.93 (5.75 points, about 6) in the 38 people with dependence at 3 or more waves. Broyd does not quote the 8-point figure.

anchors.locator: Discussion > Specificity to cannabis and potential confounds, 1st paragraph
anchors.extracted: Meier 2012 (ref 60) presented as the strongest design (premorbid ability measured): persistent use or dependence associated with an IQ decline of about 6 points, broad rather than domain-specific; cessation did not restore IQ in adolescent-onset users; specificity said to be established by ruling out recent use and persistent tobacco, alcohol and other drug use.

anchors.locator: Discussion > Persistence or recovery of function with abstinence, 3rd paragraph
anchors.extracted: Same study described as showing that use before 18 resulted in greater IQ decline by 38, persisting after cessation or reduction of use in the past year.

reporting_issues.note: Recounted from the rendered Table 1: 101 distinct reference numbers in all cells (exactly 36-58, 60-128, 142-150), 40 distinct in the acute cells, 17 in the abstinence cells (55, 57, 60, 63-67, 79, 85, 91-93, 95, 119, 127, 128).

Confirmed (refs 35 and 39 are on AM p. 14). Add: ref 67 (Winward et al., 2014) is also cited on both sides, among the studies in which working memory resolves with longer abstinence (AM p. 5) and as showing persistent working-memory deficits at 35 days (AM p. 10).
Ref 78 (Whitlow et al., 2004, on AM p. 17) is a study of long-term heavy use, inside the acute working-memory range 68-78.
Broyd's ref 3 (AM p. 12) confirmed as N Engl J Med 371:879 with three authors; Curran's ref 3 is checked in out/curran_2016.json.

risk_of_bias.note: AMSTAR 2 critically low: no protocol, two databases with a date window, no excluded-study list, no appraisal of included studies; items 11, 12 and 15 not applicable. Agree that items 5, 6 and 8 depend on the unread supplements and cannot change the overall rating.

interpretation_gap.note: Substantial: causal wording for chronic use from mostly cross-sectional, often unadjusted studies; Table 2 and the abstract stronger on persistence than Table 1 and the text; 'prolonged abstinence' mostly 3-5 weeks.

missed: Ref 67 (Winward et al., 2014) is cited both for working memory resolving with longer abstinence (AM p. 5) and for persistent working-memory deficits at 35 days (AM p. 10), like ref 85; best added to reporting issue 3.

Thames et al. (2014, ref 57) is described as abstinent at least 28 days aged about 35-50 (AM p. 7) and as abstinent more than 28 days (AM p. 10); trivial, but claims quoting the threshold should say 'about 4 weeks or more'.
